title: The infratemporal fossa
summary: The space behind the ramus where the mandibular nerve and the maxillary artery branch out around the lateral pterygoid.
objectives: Give the boundaries of the infratemporal fossa and its openings into the skull
Use the lateral pterygoid to predict where each nerve and vessel emerges
Name the branches of the mandibular nerve and the sensory territory of each
Describe the course of the chorda tympani and the lingual nerve and why they matter in dental surgery
Name the three parts of the maxillary artery and the danger of the pterygoid venous plexus
takeaways: Walls: ramus laterally, lateral pterygoid plate medially, maxilla in front, greater wing of the sphenoid above.
The lateral pterygoid is the key: the buccal nerve passes between its heads, the lingual and inferior alveolar emerge below it.
V3's anterior division is motor except the buccal nerve; its posterior division is sensory except the nerve to mylohyoid.
The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve, carrying taste from the front of the tongue and secretomotor fibres to the submandibular ganglion.
The middle meningeal artery leaves the first part of the maxillary artery; the pterygoid plexus drains to the cavernous sinus.

steps.title: A space behind the jaw
steps.text:
Take away the ramus of the mandible and you are in the infratemporal fossa. Its walls are the ramus laterally, the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid medially, the back of the maxilla anteriorly, and a roof formed by the infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid, pierced by the foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. Below and behind it is open to the neck.

Its contents are the two pterygoid muscles, the mandibular nerve and its branches, the chorda tympani, the otic ganglion, the maxillary artery and the pterygoid venous plexus.

check.q: Which two foramina open into the roof of the infratemporal fossa, and what passes through each?
check.a: Foramen ovale — the mandibular nerve (and lesser petrosal nerve); foramen spinosum — the middle meningeal artery.

steps.title: The lateral pterygoid is the landmark
steps.text:
Everything in the fossa is described relative to the lateral pterygoid, running horizontally back from the lateral pterygoid plate to the neck of the mandible and the TMJ disc. The buccal nerve emerges between its two heads; the deep temporal and masseteric nerves appear above it; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves emerge below its lower border onto the medial pterygoid. The maxillary artery runs either superficial or deep to it.

The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that opens the jaw: it pulls the condyle and disc forward onto the articular eminence.
steps.pitfall: The buccal nerve (V3, sensory to the cheek mucosa and skin) is not the nerve to buccinator — buccinator is a muscle of facial expression, supplied by the facial nerve.

check.q: Which nerve emerges between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid?
check.a: The buccal nerve.

steps.title: The mandibular nerve
steps.text: V3 leaves through the foramen ovale and, after a short trunk that gives the nerve to medial pterygoid and a meningeal branch, splits. The anterior division is motor to masseter, temporalis and lateral pterygoid, and has one sensory branch, the buccal. The posterior division is sensory: the auriculotemporal nerve, which splits around the middle meningeal artery to reach the temple; the lingual nerve; and the inferior alveolar nerve, which enters the mandibular foramen, supplies the lower teeth and ends as the mental nerve. Just before entering the foramen it gives its one motor branch, the nerve to mylohyoid.
steps.clinical: An inferior alveolar nerve block deposits anaesthetic on the medial side of the ramus above the mandibular foramen, numbing the lower teeth, lower lip and chin on that side. The lingual nerve lies just in front and is usually caught as well — a numb side of the tongue is the sign the block has worked.

check.q: Which branch of the anterior division of V3 is sensory, and which branch of the posterior division is motor?
check.a: The buccal nerve is sensory; the nerve to mylohyoid (from the inferior alveolar) is motor.

steps.title: The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve
steps.text:
The chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve in the temporal bone, crosses the middle ear on the tympanic membrane, and exits through the petrotympanic fissure to join the lingual nerve from behind. It brings two things: taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue, and preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that relay in the submandibular ganglion to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

So the lingual nerve arrives at the tongue carrying general sensation (V3) and taste (VII) together.
steps.clinical: The lingual nerve lies against the lingual cortex of the mandible beside the third molar. It can be damaged when a lower wisdom tooth is removed, leaving a numb tongue with loss of taste on that side.

check.q: A lesion of the lingual nerve above the point the chorda tympani joins it spares which function?
check.a: Taste and submandibular/sublingual secretion — those fibres join below; only general sensation of the anterior tongue is lost.

steps.title: The maxillary artery in three parts
steps.text: The larger terminal branch of the external carotid starts behind the neck of the mandible and runs forward through the fossa. It is described in three parts by the lateral pterygoid. The first (mandibular) part gives the middle meningeal artery up through the foramen spinosum and the inferior alveolar artery to the teeth. The second (pterygoid) part supplies the muscles of mastication and the buccal region. The third (pterygopalatine) part enters the pterygopalatine fossa to supply the nose, palate and upper teeth.
steps.clinical: The middle meningeal artery runs under the pterion, where the skull is thin. A blow there tears it and produces an extradural haematoma: often a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration as the lens-shaped clot expands.

check.q: From which part of the maxillary artery does the middle meningeal artery arise?
check.a: The first (mandibular) part.

steps.title: The pterygoid venous plexus
steps.text:
Around the lateral pterygoid lies a plexus of veins that drains the territory of the maxillary artery into the maxillary vein and then the retromandibular vein. It also connects, through emissary veins in the foramen ovale and through the inferior ophthalmic vein, with the cavernous sinus, and in front with the deep facial vein.

Veins here have no valves, so blood — and infection — can flow either way.
steps.clinical: A posterior superior alveolar block placed too far back can puncture the plexus and raise an alarming haematoma in the cheek within seconds. Dental and facial infections can reach the cavernous sinus the same way and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

check.q: By which routes can infection spread from the pterygoid plexus into the cranial cavity?
check.a: Through emissary veins in the foramen ovale and via the inferior ophthalmic vein into the cavernous sinus.

title: The pterygopalatine fossa
summary: A small crossroads behind the maxilla that opens into five places at once.
objectives: Give the walls of the pterygopalatine fossa and the openings from it
Trace the maxillary nerve and its main branches
Describe the inputs and outputs of the pterygopalatine ganglion
Relate the third part of the maxillary artery to epistaxis
takeaways: The fossa lies between the maxilla in front, the pterygoid process behind and the palatine bone medially.
It connects with the middle cranial fossa, orbit, nasal cavity, palate and infratemporal fossa.
V2 enters by the foramen rotundum and continues as the infraorbital nerve.
The ganglion receives the greater petrosal (VII) and deep petrosal nerves through the pterygoid canal and supplies the lacrimal gland and the glands of the nose and palate.
The sphenopalatine artery is the main source of posterior epistaxis.

steps.title: Walls and openings
steps.text: Behind the maxilla, in front of the pterygoid process of the sphenoid, and lateral to the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, is a narrow inverted pyramid. It communicates laterally with the infratemporal fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure); medially with the nasal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen); above with the orbit (inferior orbital fissure); behind with the middle cranial fossa (foramen rotundum) and the foramen lacerum region (pterygoid canal); and below with the palate (greater palatine canal).
steps.mnemonic: Think of the fossa as a junction box: one wire in from the skull (V2), one in from the face's blood supply (maxillary artery), and outputs to orbit, nose, palate and face.

check.q: Through which opening does the pterygopalatine fossa communicate with the nasal cavity?
check.a: The sphenopalatine foramen.

steps.title: The maxillary nerve
steps.text: V2 is purely sensory. It leaves the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum into the fossa, where it gives ganglionic branches (sensory fibres that pass through the ganglion without synapsing to the nose, palate and nasopharynx), the zygomatic nerve and the posterior superior alveolar nerves. It then passes through the inferior orbital fissure and runs in the floor of the orbit as the infraorbital nerve, emerging on the face below the orbit.
steps.clinical: An orbital floor ('blow-out') fracture damages the infraorbital nerve in its groove and canal: numbness of the cheek, side of the nose, upper lip and upper teeth on that side, often with an inferior rectus trapped in the fracture.

check.q: Which foramen does the maxillary nerve use to leave the skull?
check.a: The foramen rotundum.

steps.title: The pterygopalatine ganglion
steps.text: The ganglion hangs from V2 but its synapsing fibres come from the facial nerve. The greater petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) joins the deep petrosal nerve (postganglionic sympathetic, from the carotid plexus) to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal, which enters the back of the fossa. After synapsing, parasympathetic fibres ride on branches of V2 to the lacrimal gland (via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves) and to the mucous glands of the nose, palate and pharynx.
steps.clinical: Because it drives nasal secretion and lacrimation, the pterygopalatine ganglion is sometimes called the 'hay fever ganglion'; the running nose and tearing of cluster headache involve the same pathway.

check.q: A facial nerve lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion causes a dry eye. Why?
check.a: The greater petrosal nerve, which carries the secretomotor fibres for the lacrimal gland, leaves the facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion.

steps.title: The third part of the maxillary artery
steps.text: The maxillary artery enters through the pterygomaxillary fissure and breaks up with the branches of V2: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine (becoming the greater palatine artery on the hard palate), the artery of the pterygoid canal, and the sphenopalatine artery, which passes through the sphenopalatine foramen to the lateral wall and septum of the nose.
steps.clinical: Anterior epistaxis comes from Kiesselbach's plexus on the front of the septum and usually stops with pressure. Posterior epistaxis, from the sphenopalatine artery, bleeds heavily into the pharynx and may need endoscopic ligation of the artery at the sphenopalatine foramen.

check.q: Which artery is the main source of a posterior nosebleed?
check.a: The sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery.

title: The trigeminal nerve
summary: The great sensory nerve of the face, with one motor job: chewing.
objectives: Trace each division of the trigeminal nerve from the ganglion to the face
Map the three sensory territories and know where the face stops being trigeminal
List the muscles supplied by the motor root and predict the jaw deviation in a lesion
Describe the corneal and jaw jerk reflexes and the brainstem nuclei involved
Recognise trigeminal neuralgia and herpes zoster ophthalmicus
takeaways: V1 by the superior orbital fissure, V2 by the foramen rotundum, V3 by the foramen ovale.
The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–3), not the trigeminal.
V3 is motor to the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
The jaw deviates towards the side of a V3 motor lesion.
The spinal trigeminal nucleus descends into the upper cervical cord, so a lateral medullary lesion numbs the face on the same side.

steps.title: One ganglion, three divisions
steps.text: The trigeminal nerve leaves the side of the pons as a large sensory root and a small motor root. The sensory root expands into the trigeminal ganglion, lying in a dural pocket (Meckel's cave) on the apex of the petrous temporal bone. From it three divisions leave the skull: ophthalmic (V1) through the superior orbital fissure, maxillary (V2) through the foramen rotundum, and mandibular (V3) through the foramen ovale, joined by the motor root.

check.q: Through which openings do V1, V2 and V3 leave the skull?
check.a: Superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum and foramen ovale.

steps.title: The ophthalmic division
steps.text: V1 is sensory to the forehead and scalp as far back as the vertex, the upper eyelid, the cornea and conjunctiva, and the bridge and tip of the nose. In the orbit it splits into the frontal nerve (supra-orbital and supratrochlear), the lacrimal nerve, and the nasociliary nerve, which gives the long ciliary nerves to the cornea and ends as the external nasal nerve at the tip of the nose.
steps.clinical: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus reactivates in the trigeminal ganglion and erupts along V1. When the nasociliary branch is involved the cornea and uvea are at risk, and urgent ophthalmological review is needed.

check.q: What is Hutchinson's sign?
check.a: Vesicles on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster of V1 — the nasociliary nerve is involved, so the eye is likely to be affected too.

steps.title: The maxillary and mandibular skin
steps.text:
V2 supplies the lower eyelid, the cheek, the side of the nose and the upper lip, as well as the upper teeth, palate and most of the nasal cavity. V3 supplies the lower lip and chin, the lower teeth and gums, the front of the ear and the temple (auriculotemporal nerve), and general sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue (lingual nerve).

Below and behind that, the skin over the angle of the mandible and most of the ear is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–3).
steps.pitfall: The trigeminal territory does not extend onto the angle of the jaw or the back of the scalp; the boundary is a useful check on the anatomy of a reported sensory loss.

check.q: A patient reports numbness of the whole face including the angle of the jaw. What does the angle tell you?
check.a: The angle is supplied by C2–3 (great auricular), not the trigeminal nerve — a loss that includes it is not explained by a trigeminal lesion.

steps.title: The motor root: chewing and a little more
steps.text:
The motor root travels with V3 and supplies the four muscles of mastication — masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid — together with mylohyoid, the anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini: every muscle derived from the first pharyngeal arch.

The two lateral pterygoids protrude the jaw together; one alone swings the chin to the opposite side.
steps.clinical: Wasting of temporalis and masseter is felt as hollowing of the temple and cheek when the patient clenches.

check.q: After a right V3 motor lesion, which way does the jaw deviate on opening, and why?
check.a: To the right — the intact left lateral pterygoid pushes the left condyle forward unopposed, swinging the chin towards the weak side.

steps.title: Reflexes and the long sensory nucleus
steps.text:
The trigeminal sensory nucleus runs the length of the brainstem. Its principal part in the pons handles touch; the spinal trigeminal nucleus descends through the medulla into the upper cervical cord and handles pain and temperature; the mesencephalic nucleus carries proprioception from the jaw muscles.

The corneal reflex is afferent V1, efferent VII, and both eyes blink. The jaw jerk is V3 in both directions; it is brisk when the corticobulbar pathways are damaged on both sides.
steps.clinical: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome gives ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss with contralateral loss over the body — a crossed pattern that localises the lesion to the medulla.

check.q: Why does a lateral medullary infarct cause loss of pain sensation on the same side of the face?
check.a: It damages the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, which carry pain and temperature from the ipsilateral face before any crossing.

steps.title: Trigeminal neuralgia
steps.text: Paroxysms of electric, stabbing pain lasting seconds in the territory of V2 or V3, triggered by touching the face, chewing, shaving or a cold wind — and nothing between attacks. In most cases an artery, typically the superior cerebellar artery, is compressing the nerve root where it enters the pons and its myelin changes from peripheral to central.
steps.clinical: Carbamazepine is first-line. Microvascular decompression moves the vessel off the root. In a young patient, or with bilateral symptoms, think of multiple sclerosis with a plaque at the root entry zone.

check.q: Where along the nerve is the compression in classical trigeminal neuralgia?
check.a: At the root entry zone at the pons, usually by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery.

title: The nerves of eye movement: III, IV and VI
summary: Three nerves, six muscles, and the palsies that tell you where to look.
objectives: State which nerve supplies each extra-ocular muscle
Describe the relations of III, IV and VI in the cavernous sinus
Distinguish a compressive from an ischaemic oculomotor palsy by the pupil
Describe the diplopia and head posture of a trochlear and an abducens palsy
Test each muscle in the position that isolates it
takeaways: LR6 SO4, the rest 3 — and levator palpebrae is III too.
In the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus: III, IV, V1, V2; within it, the ICA with VI beside it.
A painful III palsy with a dilated pupil is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proved otherwise.
IV palsy: vertical diplopia worst looking down and in; head tilted away from the lesion.
VI palsy: horizontal diplopia worse towards the lesion; a false localising sign of raised pressure.

steps.title: Three nerves, six muscles
steps.text: The abducens nerve (VI) supplies lateral rectus. The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies superior oblique. The oculomotor nerve (III) supplies everything else: superior, inferior and medial rectus, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris — and carries the parasympathetic fibres that constrict the pupil and accommodate the lens.

check.q: Which extra-ocular muscles does the oculomotor nerve supply?
check.a: Superior, inferior and medial rectus, inferior oblique — plus levator palpebrae superioris.

steps.title: Through the cavernous sinus
steps.text: All three nerves pass through the cavernous sinus beside the sella. In its lateral wall, from above down, run III, IV, V1 and V2. Inside the sinus, bathed in venous blood, are the internal carotid artery and, lateral to it, the abducens nerve. They then enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
steps.clinical: In cavernous sinus thrombosis — often spread from a facial or sinus infection — the abducens is usually affected first, so a lateral gaze palsy may precede ophthalmoplegia, proptosis and chemosis. A carotid–cavernous fistula gives a pulsating eye with a bruit.

check.q: Which cranial nerve lies free within the cavernous sinus rather than in its wall?
check.a: The abducens nerve (VI), beside the internal carotid artery.

steps.title: The oculomotor nerve and the pupil
steps.text:
III leaves the midbrain in the interpeduncular fossa and passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, then alongside the posterior communicating artery. A complete palsy leaves the eye down and out (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

The pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, nearest a compressing lesion, while its core depends on small vasa nervorum.
steps.clinical: A new III palsy with a dilated pupil is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proved otherwise and needs urgent vascular imaging. A dilating pupil in a drowsy patient signals uncal herniation compressing III against the tentorium.

check.q: A diabetic patient has a painful III palsy but a normal pupil. Why is that reassuring?
check.a: Microvascular infarction affects the core of the nerve and spares the superficial pupillary fibres; compression, as by an aneurysm, affects the pupil first.

steps.title: The trochlear nerve
steps.text:
IV is the thinnest cranial nerve, the only one to leave the back of the brainstem, and the only one whose fibres cross before leaving — so the right trochlear nucleus supplies the left superior oblique. It has the longest intracranial course, winding round the midbrain.

The superior oblique passes through its pulley, the trochlea, and pulls the back of the eye up: it depresses the eye most effectively when it is adducted, and it intorts.
steps.clinical: Its long, thin course makes IV vulnerable to head injury, and the patient may present only with difficulty on stairs or an unexplained head tilt in old photographs (congenital palsy).

check.q: In a left trochlear palsy, which way does the patient tilt the head, and when is the diplopia worst?
check.a: Towards the right (away from the lesion), to reduce the need for intorsion; diplopia is vertical and worst looking down and to the right — reading or going downstairs.

steps.title: The abducens nerve
steps.text: VI leaves the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction and climbs the clivus, bending sharply over the petrous apex beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament before entering the cavernous sinus. A palsy stops abduction: the eye rests turned in and the patient sees horizontal diplopia, worse looking towards the side of the lesion.
steps.clinical: Bilateral abducens palsies with headache and papilloedema suggest raised pressure, for example idiopathic intracranial hypertension, rather than a lesion at the nerve itself.

check.q: Why can raised intracranial pressure cause a VI palsy even when the lesion is far away?
check.a: Downward displacement of the brainstem stretches the nerve over the petrous apex — a false localising sign.

steps.title: Testing the muscles one by one
steps.text: The recti and obliques have mixed actions in the primary position, so clinical testing puts the eye where one muscle acts alone. Superior and inferior rectus are tested with the eye abducted, where they are pure elevator and depressor. The obliques are tested with the eye adducted: inferior oblique elevates it, superior oblique depresses it. Medial and lateral rectus are tested with simple horizontal movement. The result is the familiar H-shaped test.
steps.pitfall: The anatomical action of superior oblique is depression, abduction and intorsion, but it is tested looking down and in. Do not confuse the textbook action with the test position.

check.q: With the eye adducted, which muscle depresses it?
check.a: The superior oblique.

title: The vagus nerve
summary: The wanderer: from the medulla to the splenic flexure, with a detour round the aortic arch.
objectives: Follow the vagus from the jugular foramen through neck, thorax and abdomen
Name its branches in the neck and what each supplies
Explain why the two recurrent laryngeal nerves take different routes
Describe the oesophageal plexus and the vagal trunks
Describe the sensory side of the vagus and the reflexes it carries
takeaways: The vagus runs in the carotid sheath, behind and between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.
Pharyngeal branch: palate and pharynx. Superior laryngeal: internal (sensation above the cords) and external (cricothyroid).
The right recurrent laryngeal hooks under the subclavian artery; the left under the aortic arch.
Left vagus becomes the anterior trunk, right the posterior (LARP), through the oesophageal hiatus at T10.
Most vagal fibres are afferent; parasympathetic supply of the gut reaches the midgut and stops at the splenic flexure.

steps.title: From the medulla to the carotid sheath
steps.text: The vagus leaves the side of the medulla in a row of rootlets and passes through the jugular foramen with IX and XI, swelling into superior and inferior ganglia. In the neck it runs in the carotid sheath, posterior and between the internal jugular vein and the internal then common carotid artery.

check.q: What is the position of the vagus in the carotid sheath?
check.a: Posterior, in the groove between the internal jugular vein laterally and the carotid artery medially.

steps.title: Branches in the neck
steps.text: The pharyngeal branch supplies the muscles of the pharynx and soft palate (except stylopharyngeus, IX, and tensor veli palatini, V3). The superior laryngeal nerve divides into an internal branch, which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and gives sensation above the vocal folds, and an external branch to cricothyroid, which runs close to the superior thyroid artery. Cardiac branches descend to the cardiac plexus.
steps.clinical: Tying the superior thyroid artery high at thyroidectomy can catch the external laryngeal nerve: the voice tires and loses its upper range, a problem that matters most to singers. A vagal lesion makes the uvula deviate away from the weak side.

check.q: Which laryngeal muscle is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and what supplies it?
check.a: Cricothyroid, supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

steps.title: The two recurrent laryngeal nerves
steps.text: On the right the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery; on the left it hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum. Both then climb in the groove between trachea and oesophagus, pass behind the thyroid lobe and enter the larynx to supply all its intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, and sensation below the cords.
steps.clinical: Hoarseness from a left vocal cord palsy can be the first sign of a lung cancer at the left hilum. The asymmetry is embryological: the nerves hook under the sixth arch arteries, and on the right the distal sixth arch disappears.

check.q: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve damaged by diseases of the chest?
check.a: It descends into the thorax and hooks under the aortic arch, so an aortic aneurysm, a hilar lung cancer, enlarged mediastinal nodes or a large left atrium can compress it.

steps.title: In the thorax: the oesophageal plexus
steps.text:
Each vagus passes behind the root of the lung, giving pulmonary branches, and reaches the oesophagus, where the two nerves break up into the oesophageal plexus. At the lower end the plexus regroups into an anterior vagal trunk, mainly from the left vagus, and a posterior vagal trunk, mainly from the right. Both pass through the oesophageal hiatus at T10.

The rotation of the stomach in the embryo explains the swap.
steps.clinical: Vagal cardiac branches slow the sinoatrial node and atrioventricular conduction; carotid sinus massage and the Valsalva manoeuvre work through them to end a supraventricular tachycardia.

check.q: Which vagal trunk lies on the front of the oesophagus at the hiatus?
check.a: The anterior trunk, derived mainly from the left vagus.

steps.title: In the abdomen
steps.text: The anterior trunk supplies the front of the stomach and gives a hepatic branch; the posterior trunk supplies the back of the stomach and sends a large coeliac branch onwards with the arteries. Vagal parasympathetic fibres reach the whole foregut and midgut — as far as about two thirds of the way along the transverse colon. Beyond that the hindgut is supplied by the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4).
steps.clinical: Truncal vagotomy, once used for peptic ulcer, reduced acid but also left the pylorus unable to relax, so a drainage procedure had to be added. Highly selective vagotomy spared the nerves of Latarjet to the pylorus.

check.q: Where does the vagal parasympathetic supply to the gut stop, and what takes over?
check.a: Near the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the transverse colon (the end of the midgut); the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–4) take over.

steps.title: Mostly a sensory nerve
steps.text: About four fifths of vagal fibres are afferent. They carry stretch from the lungs and gut, pressure from the aortic arch baroreceptors, chemical signals from the aortic bodies, sensation from the larynx and lower pharynx, and — through a small auricular branch — sensation from part of the external acoustic meatus.
steps.clinical: The afferent limb of the cough reflex, of vomiting, and of vasovagal syncope all run in the vagus. Its afferents are the target of vagus nerve stimulation used for refractory epilepsy.

check.q: Why can cleaning the ear canal make a patient cough or faint?
check.a: The auricular branch of the vagus supplies part of the external acoustic meatus, so stimulating it can trigger vagal reflexes.

title: Glossopharyngeal, accessory and hypoglossal
summary: The last three cranial nerves, how to test them, and how to tell bulbar from pseudobulbar palsy.
objectives: Describe the sensory, motor and parasympathetic components of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Describe the course of the accessory nerve in the posterior triangle and the effect of injuring it
Describe the course of the hypoglossal nerve and the direction of tongue deviation
Recognise a jugular foramen syndrome
Distinguish bulbar from pseudobulbar palsy
takeaways: IX: taste and sensation from the back of the tongue, the carotid sinus, stylopharyngeus, and the parotid via the otic ganglion.
The gag reflex: IX in, X out.
XI crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is easily cut; trapezius is lost, sternocleidomastoid spared.
The tongue deviates towards the side of a hypoglossal lesion.
Bulbar palsy is lower motor neuron (wasted, fasciculating tongue); pseudobulbar is upper motor neuron (small spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk).

steps.title: The glossopharyngeal nerve
steps.text:
IX leaves the medulla and the skull through the jugular foramen. It is mostly sensory: taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, sensation from the oropharynx, tonsil and middle ear, and signals from the carotid sinus and carotid body. Its only muscle is stylopharyngeus, the muscle of the third arch.

Its parasympathetic fibres reach the parotid gland by a roundabout route: tympanic nerve, lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion, then the auriculotemporal nerve.

check.q: Which is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
check.a: Stylopharyngeus.

steps.title: The gag reflex and the jugular foramen
steps.text: Touching the back of the pharynx provokes a gag: the afferent limb is IX, the efferent is X. Because IX, X and XI share the jugular foramen with the internal jugular vein, a lesion there — a glomus jugulare tumour, a skull-base fracture or metastasis — damages all three together.
steps.clinical: If XII is also involved, the lesion is more likely below the skull, in the retrostyloid space, where all four nerves lie together.

check.q: A patient has an absent gag, hoarseness, dysphagia and a weak shrug on the same side. Where is the lesion?
check.a: At the jugular foramen, affecting IX, X and XI together (jugular foramen or Vernet syndrome).

steps.title: The accessory nerve
steps.text: The spinal accessory nerve arises from the upper five cervical segments, climbs through the foramen magnum and leaves again by the jugular foramen. It supplies sternocleidomastoid, passing through or deep to it, then crosses the posterior triangle — lying superficially on levator scapulae, just under the investing fascia — to reach trapezius.
steps.clinical: Accessory nerve injury is one of the commonest iatrogenic nerve injuries. Trapezius paralysis causes a dropped shoulder, weak abduction above 90° and lateral winging of the scapula, and aches from the dragging.

check.q: After a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle a patient cannot shrug and the shoulder droops, but head turning is normal. Why?
check.a: The accessory nerve was cut in the posterior triangle, after it had already supplied sternocleidomastoid; only trapezius is paralysed.

steps.title: The hypoglossal nerve
steps.text:
XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal, descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, then turns forward, crossing the internal and external carotid arteries superficially just above the hyoid, to run on hyoglossus into the tongue. It supplies all the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (X).

C1 fibres hitch-hike on it and leave as the upper root of the ansa cervicalis and the nerves to geniohyoid and thyrohyoid.
steps.mnemonic: The tongue licks its wounds: it deviates towards the side of a lower motor neuron lesion.
steps.clinical: It is at risk in carotid endarterectomy and submandibular gland surgery, where it runs just deep to the operative field.

check.q: Which way does the tongue point on protrusion after a right hypoglossal nerve lesion?
check.a: To the right — the left genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and across, unopposed.

steps.title: Bulbar or pseudobulbar?
steps.text: Both cause difficulty speaking and swallowing. Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neuron problem — the nuclei of IX–XII in the medulla (the 'bulb') or their nerves: the tongue is wasted and fasciculates, speech is nasal, the gag reflex is lost and the jaw jerk is normal. Pseudobulbar palsy is bilateral upper motor neuron damage to the corticobulbar tracts: the tongue is small and stiff, speech is slow and strained, the jaw jerk is brisk, and emotional lability is common.
steps.clinical: Motor neurone disease can produce both at once. Bilateral strokes and multiple sclerosis produce pseudobulbar palsy; Guillain–Barré, myasthenia and brainstem lesions produce bulbar palsy.

check.q: A patient has a small spastic tongue and a brisk jaw jerk. Bulbar or pseudobulbar?
check.a: Pseudobulbar — bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) disease.

title: The visual pathway and its field defects
summary: From retina to occipital pole — draw the pathway once and every field defect follows.
objectives: Explain which retinal fibres cross at the chiasm and why
Predict the field defect from a lesion of the optic nerve, chiasm, tract, radiation and cortex
Explain why the pupillary reflex survives a lesion behind the lateral geniculate body
Describe macular sparing and its blood supply
takeaways: Nasal fibres cross, temporal fibres do not — each hemisphere sees the opposite half of the world.
Nerve: monocular loss. Chiasm: bitemporal hemianopia. Behind the chiasm: contralateral homonymous defects.
Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe carries the upper field: temporal lesions give a superior quadrantanopia.
Pupillary fibres leave the tract before the lateral geniculate body.
The occipital pole has a dual MCA and PCA supply, so a PCA infarct often spares the macula.

steps.title: Half the fibres cross
steps.text:
Each retina is divided into a nasal and a temporal half. The nasal half sees the temporal field and its fibres cross at the chiasm; the temporal half sees the nasal field and stays on the same side. After the chiasm each optic tract carries the whole of the opposite visual field from both eyes.

Remember that the retina sees the world inverted and reversed: the upper field falls on the lower retina, the left field on the right half of each retina.

check.q: Which retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
check.a: Those from the nasal half of each retina (carrying the temporal visual field).

steps.title: The optic nerve
steps.text:
The optic nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a tract of the brain: its axons are myelinated by oligodendrocytes and it is wrapped in all three meninges, with subarachnoid space and CSF around it all the way to the eye. It leaves the orbit through the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery.

A lesion here causes loss of vision in one eye and a relative afferent pupillary defect: swinging a torch to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate.
steps.clinical: Optic neuritis, often the first event in multiple sclerosis, gives painful loss of vision in one eye with poor colour vision and an afferent pupillary defect.

check.q: Why does raised intracranial pressure make the optic disc swell?
check.a: The subarachnoid space extends along the optic nerve, so raised CSF pressure compresses the nerve and obstructs axoplasmic flow and venous return at the disc — papilloedema.

steps.title: The chiasm and the pituitary
steps.text: The optic chiasm lies above the diaphragma sellae and the pituitary gland. A pituitary adenoma growing up out of the sella presses on the crossing fibres from below — the fibres from the inferior nasal retina — first. The result is a bitemporal hemianopia that usually starts in the upper temporal quadrants.
steps.clinical: A craniopharyngioma pressing from above tends to affect the lower temporal quadrants first. Bitemporal loss is easily missed because each eye's nasal field fills the other's gap — test each eye separately.

check.q: Why does a pituitary adenoma typically cause a bitemporal defect that begins in the upper fields?
check.a: It compresses the crossing nasal fibres from below, and the lower nasal fibres (which see the upper temporal field) cross lowest in the chiasm.

steps.title: The optic tract and the lateral geniculate body
steps.text: Each optic tract winds round the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus. A tract lesion gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous. Before reaching the lateral geniculate body, the fibres for the pupillary light reflex leave to the pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei.

check.q: A patient is cortically blind but the pupils still react to light. How is that possible?
check.a: The pupillary fibres leave the optic tract before the lateral geniculate body, so the reflex arc bypasses the radiation and the visual cortex.

steps.title: The optic radiation
steps.text: From the lateral geniculate body the optic radiation fans back to the occipital cortex. Fibres for the lower retina — the upper field — loop forward into the temporal lobe around the temporal horn (Meyer's loop). Fibres for the upper retina — the lower field — run straight back through the parietal lobe.
steps.clinical: Meyer's loop is at risk in temporal lobectomy for epilepsy, and patients are warned of an upper quadrant defect.

check.q: A temporal lobe tumour on the left produces which field defect?
check.a: A right (contralateral) homonymous superior quadrantanopia — 'pie in the sky'.

steps.title: The visual cortex and macular sparing
steps.text:
The primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe. The cuneus above it receives the lower field; the lingual gyrus below receives the upper field. The macula has an enormous representation at the occipital pole.

The calcarine cortex is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, but the pole often also receives branches of the middle cerebral artery.
steps.clinical: Homonymous hemianopia is the commonest visual consequence of stroke. Patients may be unaware of it, bumping into things on one side, and it bars driving.

check.q: Why does a posterior cerebral artery infarct often give a hemianopia with macular sparing?
check.a: The occipital pole, where the macula is represented, frequently has a collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery that survives.

title: The pituitary and hypothalamus
summary: A gland the size of a pea in a bony cup, with the optic chiasm above and a sinus of veins on either side.
objectives: Describe the relations of the pituitary in the sella turcica
Explain the different origins of the anterior and posterior pituitary
Describe the hypophyseal portal system and the stalk effect
Name the hypothalamic nuclei that make ADH and oxytocin
Predict the effects of a pituitary tumour growing in each direction
takeaways: Above: diaphragma sellae and optic chiasm. Either side: cavernous sinuses. Below: sphenoid sinus.
The adenohypophysis comes from Rathke's pouch; the neurohypophysis is a downgrowth of the diencephalon.
Releasing hormones reach the anterior lobe by portal veins in the stalk; dopamine holds prolactin down.
ADH and oxytocin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the posterior lobe.
A tumour growing up gives bitemporal hemianopia; sideways, cranial nerve palsies; down, it can be reached through the nose.

steps.title: In the sella turcica
steps.text: The hypophysis sits in the sella turcica ('Turkish saddle') of the sphenoid bone, roofed by a fold of dura, the diaphragma sellae, which the stalk pierces. Above lies the optic chiasm; on each side the cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery and nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI; below and in front the air-filled sphenoid sinus.

check.q: What lies directly below the pituitary fossa, and why is that useful to surgeons?
check.a: The sphenoid sinus — the pituitary can be approached through the nose and the sinus (the transsphenoidal route) without opening the cranium.

steps.title: Two glands in one
steps.text: The adenohypophysis (anterior lobe) grows up from the roof of the embryonic mouth as Rathke's pouch — it is glandular epithelium. The neurohypophysis (posterior lobe and stalk) grows down from the floor of the diencephalon — it is nervous tissue, mostly the axons of hypothalamic neurons and their supporting pituicytes. The two meet and fuse, but never mix.
steps.clinical: Remnants of Rathke's pouch can give rise to a craniopharyngioma, typically in children, a calcified cystic mass above the sella that presses on the chiasm and hypothalamus.

check.q: From which embryonic tissue does the anterior pituitary develop?
check.a: From Rathke's pouch, an outgrowth of the ectoderm of the roof of the primitive mouth.

steps.title: The portal system and the stalk
steps.text:
Hypothalamic neurons release their releasing and inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) into a capillary bed at the median eminence. Portal veins down the stalk carry them to a second capillary bed in the anterior lobe, where they act on the endocrine cells at high concentration.

Most control is stimulatory — except prolactin, which is held down by dopamine.
steps.clinical: Dopamine-blocking drugs such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin by the same mechanism, causing galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea.

check.q: Why can a non-secreting tumour that compresses the pituitary stalk raise the prolactin level?
check.a: It interrupts dopamine reaching the anterior lobe through the portal veins, releasing the lactotrophs from inhibition — the stalk effect.

steps.title: The posterior lobe
steps.text: The posterior lobe makes nothing. Its hormones are made in the cell bodies of large neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus — ADH (vasopressin) mainly supraoptic, oxytocin mainly paraventricular — carried down their axons in the stalk, and released into capillaries of the posterior lobe.
steps.clinical: Central diabetes insipidus follows pituitary surgery, head injury and hypothalamic tumours; it responds to desmopressin. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not.

check.q: After a head injury a patient passes several litres of dilute urine a day. What is the likely cause?
check.a: Central diabetes insipidus — damage to the stalk or hypothalamus stops ADH release.

steps.title: Which way a tumour grows
steps.text: Pituitary adenomas cause trouble in two ways: by what they secrete — prolactin (the commonest), growth hormone (acromegaly) or ACTH (Cushing disease) — and by what they press on. Growing upwards they compress the chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and eventually the hypothalamus. Growing sideways into the cavernous sinus they involve III, IV and VI. Squeezing the normal gland causes hypopituitarism, with GH and gonadotrophins failing first.
steps.clinical: Pituitary apoplexy — sudden haemorrhage into an adenoma — presents with thunderclap headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia, and life-threatening acute cortisol deficiency.

check.q: A pituitary tumour invades the right cavernous sinus. Which nerves are at risk?
check.a: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI on the right, with the internal carotid artery encased.

steps.title: The pineal gland
steps.text: Behind the third ventricle, above the superior colliculi, lies the pineal gland. It secretes melatonin at night, driven through a pathway from the retina via the suprachiasmatic nucleus and the sympathetic chain, and helps set circadian rhythm. It calcifies with age, which makes it a useful midline marker on a skull film or CT.

check.q: Why does a pineal tumour cause paralysis of upward gaze?
check.a: It compresses the dorsal midbrain (tectum) beneath it, producing Parinaud syndrome; it can also block the cerebral aqueduct and cause hydrocephalus.

title: The root of the neck and the thoracic inlet
summary: Where the neck, thorax and upper limb meet — and where central lines, blocks and tumours go wrong.
objectives: Give the boundaries of the thoracic inlet and the height of the cervical pleura
Use scalenus anterior to place the subclavian artery, vein and brachial plexus
Name the branches of the subclavian artery
Describe the formation of the brachiocephalic veins and the venous angle
Explain the signs of a tumour at the lung apex
takeaways: The cervical pleura and lung apex rise 2–3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle.
The subclavian vein passes in front of scalenus anterior; the artery and the brachial plexus trunks behind it.
Subclavian branches: vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical, costocervical, dorsal scapular.
The internal jugular and subclavian veins join behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein.
A Pancoast tumour can cause Horner syndrome, T1 wasting and arm pain together.

steps.title: The inlet and the dome of pleura
steps.text: The thoracic inlet is the ring bounded by the body of T1, the first ribs and their cartilages, and the top of the manubrium. It slopes forward and down, so the cervical pleura and the apex of the lung rise into the neck, 2–3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, covered by a thickened fascia (the suprapleural membrane).

check.q: Why is a pneumothorax a recognised complication of a supraclavicular brachial plexus block or a subclavian line?
check.a: The cervical pleura and lung apex lie above the medial clavicle, within reach of a needle aimed at the plexus or vein.

steps.title: Scalenus anterior is the key
steps.text: Scalenus anterior runs from the cervical transverse processes to the scalene tubercle of the first rib. The subclavian vein crosses the rib in front of it. The subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind it, through the gap between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius. The phrenic nerve runs down on its front surface.
steps.clinical: In thoracic outlet syndrome a cervical rib or fibrous band narrows this gap, compressing the lower trunk (T1 symptoms along the ulnar side of the forearm and hand) or the artery. The interscalene block injects local anaesthetic into the same gap.

check.q: What passes between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius?
check.a: The subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus (the interscalene gap).

steps.title: Branches of the subclavian artery
steps.text: Scalenus anterior divides the artery into three parts. From the first part arise the vertebral artery (up to the foramen transversarium of C6), the internal thoracic artery (down behind the costal cartilages) and the thyrocervical trunk (inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical). The costocervical trunk arises from the second part on the right (often the first on the left), and the dorsal scapular artery commonly from the third.
steps.mnemonic: VIT C, D: Vertebral, Internal thoracic, Thyrocervical, Costocervical, Dorsal scapular.
steps.clinical: In subclavian steal, a stenosis before the vertebral origin makes arm exercise draw blood backwards down the vertebral artery from the basilar system, causing dizziness. The internal thoracic artery is the preferred graft for the left anterior descending artery.

check.q: Name the branches of the subclavian artery.
check.a: Vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk and dorsal scapular.

steps.title: The veins and the venous angle
steps.text: Behind each sternoclavicular joint the internal jugular and subclavian veins join to form the brachiocephalic vein. The left brachiocephalic vein is long, crossing obliquely behind the manubrium in front of the arch branches to join the right and form the superior vena cava. At the junction on the left — the venous angle — the thoracic duct empties; the right lymphatic duct does the same on the right.
steps.clinical: Central lines are placed in the internal jugular vein under ultrasound, at the apex of the triangle between the two heads of sternocleidomastoid. A left-sided line or neck operation can injure the thoracic duct and cause a chylous leak.

check.q: Where do the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet?
check.a: Behind the sternoclavicular joint, forming the brachiocephalic vein.

steps.title: The apex of the lung and the sympathetic chain
steps.text: Behind the dome of pleura lie the neck of the first rib, the sympathetic trunk with its cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion, and the T1 root of the brachial plexus. A tumour at the apex — a Pancoast tumour — can involve all of them.
steps.clinical: Horner syndrome is ptosis (loss of the smooth-muscle part of levator), miosis and anhidrosis on the same side. A stellate ganglion block produces it deliberately and is used for some pain syndromes.

check.q: Which triad suggests a tumour at the apex of the lung?
check.a: Horner syndrome (sympathetic chain), wasting of the small hand muscles (T1) and pain in the shoulder and inner arm.

title: The pharyngeal arches and what they become
summary: Five arches, four pouches, one rule: the nerve of the arch supplies every muscle it makes.
objectives: List the nerve, cartilage derivatives and muscles of each pharyngeal arch
Explain adult nerve supply patterns from their arch of origin
Name the derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches
Explain the adult position of the parathyroids and the path of the thyroid
Recognise branchial and thyroglossal anomalies
takeaways: Arch 1 (V3): malleus, incus, muscles of mastication. Arch 2 (VII): stapes, styloid, muscles of facial expression.
Arch 3 (IX): stylopharyngeus and the lower hyoid. Arches 4 and 6 (X): larynx and pharynx.
Pouch 1: middle ear. 2: tonsil. 3: inferior parathyroid and thymus. 4: superior parathyroid.
The third pouch parathyroid ends up lower because it migrates with the thymus.
Branchial cysts lie at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; thyroglossal cysts are midline and rise on tongue protrusion.

steps.title: A segmented neck
steps.text:
In the fourth and fifth weeks the side of the embryonic pharynx bulges into a series of pharyngeal arches, separated outside by ectodermal clefts and inside by endodermal pouches. Each arch has its own cartilage, artery, muscle mass and cranial nerve. The arches are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 — the fifth is rudimentary.

The muscle of an arch keeps its nerve for life, wherever it ends up. That is the key to the apparently odd nerve supply of the head and neck.

check.q: Which cranial nerve belongs to each of arches 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6?
check.a: 1 — trigeminal (V3); 2 — facial; 3 — glossopharyngeal; 4 — vagus (superior laryngeal); 6 — vagus (recurrent laryngeal).

steps.title: The first arch
steps.text: The first arch forms the maxillary and mandibular processes. Its cartilage (Meckel's) gives the malleus and incus and the sphenomandibular ligament; the mandible itself forms by membrane ossification around it. Its muscles are the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, the anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini — all supplied by V3.
steps.clinical: Failure of neural crest migration into the first arch underlies Treacher Collins syndrome (small mandible and zygoma, ear anomalies) and the Pierre Robin sequence.

check.q: Why is tensor tympani supplied by the trigeminal nerve?
check.a: It is a first-arch muscle, and the nerve of the first arch is the mandibular division of the trigeminal.

steps.title: The second arch
steps.text: The second arch's cartilage (Reichert's) gives the stapes, the styloid process, the stylohyoid ligament and the lesser horn and upper body of the hyoid. Its muscle mass spreads out over the face and scalp as the muscles of facial expression, and also forms stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric — all supplied by the facial nerve.

check.q: Why are the two bellies of digastric supplied by different nerves?
check.a: The anterior belly comes from the first arch (V3, nerve to mylohyoid); the posterior belly from the second (facial nerve).

steps.title: The third, fourth and sixth arches
steps.text:
The third arch gives the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid and one muscle, stylopharyngeus (IX); its artery becomes the common and internal carotid. The fourth and sixth arches give the laryngeal cartilages. The fourth arch muscles are the pharyngeal constrictors and cricothyroid, supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve; the sixth arch muscles are the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

The fourth arch arteries form the aortic arch (left) and proximal right subclavian; the sixth form the pulmonary arteries and the ductus arteriosus.

check.q: Why does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hook under the aortic arch?
check.a: It hooks under the sixth arch artery, which on the left persists as the ductus (ligamentum) arteriosus beside the arch; on the right that artery regresses and the nerve rises to the fourth arch artery, the subclavian.

steps.title: The pouches
steps.text:
The first pouch forms the tympanic cavity and auditory tube. The second forms the crypts of the palatine tonsil. The third forms the inferior parathyroid and the thymus. The fourth forms the superior parathyroid and the ultimobranchial body, which supplies the thyroid's C cells.

The thymus migrates down into the mediastinum and drags the third pouch parathyroid with it, overtaking the fourth pouch gland.
steps.clinical: An inferior parathyroid adenoma may lie anywhere along the thymic descent, even in the mediastinum. In DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) the third and fourth pouches fail: hypocalcaemia, T-cell deficiency and conotruncal heart defects.

check.q: Why does the parathyroid from the third pouch end up below the one from the fourth?
check.a: It migrates caudally with the thymus, which descends into the thorax.

steps.title: Clefts, cysts and the thyroglossal duct
steps.text:
Only the first cleft persists, as the external acoustic meatus. The second arch grows down over the others, burying clefts 2–4 in a temporary cervical sinus. A remnant forms a branchial cyst, a smooth swelling at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult.

The thyroid develops in the midline at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends in front of the hyoid, trailing the thyroglossal duct. Its lower end may persist as a pyramidal lobe.
steps.clinical: Excision of a thyroglossal cyst must include the central part of the hyoid body and the tract up to the foramen caecum (Sistrunk operation), or it recurs.

check.q: A midline neck lump moves up when the patient sticks out the tongue. What is it?
check.a: A thyroglossal cyst — it is tethered to the tongue base by the remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

title: The larynx in the clinic
summary: Where to cut in an emergency, what the cords do after nerve injury, and where tumours spread.
objectives: Locate the cricothyroid membrane by palpation and explain why it is the emergency airway
Describe the sensory division of the larynx at the vocal folds
Predict the position of a paralysed vocal fold
Relate the lymphatic drainage of the larynx to the behaviour of glottic and supraglottic cancer
takeaways: Feel the thyroid prominence, slide down to the gap before the cricoid: that is the cricothyroid membrane.
Internal laryngeal nerve above the folds, recurrent laryngeal below.
A unilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy leaves the cord near the midline: hoarse voice, airway preserved.
Bilateral palsy leaves both cords near the midline: good voice, stridor.
The vocal folds have almost no lymphatics, so glottic cancer presents early and spreads late.

steps.title: Finding the cricothyroid membrane
steps.text: Run a finger down the midline of the neck: the hyoid, then the notch and prominence of the thyroid cartilage, then a soft dip, then the firm ring of the cricoid cartilage. The dip is the median cricothyroid ligament (membrane). It is superficial, avascular apart from small cricothyroid branches, and lies below the vocal folds.
steps.clinical: In a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' emergency, a scalpel cricothyroidotomy through this membrane restores oxygenation. In children the cricoid is the narrowest point and needle techniques are preferred.

check.q: Why is the cricothyroid membrane used for an emergency surgical airway rather than the trachea?
check.a: It is superficial, easy to feel, relatively avascular and below the vocal folds, whereas the trachea is deeper and covered by the thyroid isthmus and veins.

steps.title: Sensation above and below the folds
steps.text: The mucosa of the larynx above the vocal folds, including the epiglottis and the vestibule, is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve, which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. Below the folds the mucosa is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The supraglottic mucosa is exquisitely sensitive — the trigger for the cough that protects the airway.

check.q: Where can the internal laryngeal nerve be blocked for awake fibreoptic intubation?
check.a: Where it pierces the thyrohyoid membrane, just below the greater horn of the hyoid.

steps.title: Where a paralysed cord lies
steps.text: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the cords. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies it and all the other intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid. After a unilateral recurrent laryngeal injury the cord lies near the midline (paramedian): the voice is weak and breathy, but the airway is adequate because the other cord still abducts.
steps.clinical: Both nerves are at risk in total thyroidectomy, where they lie in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to the inferior thyroid artery. Bilateral injury may need an emergency tracheostomy.

check.q: Why does bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy cause stridor but a relatively good voice?
check.a: Both cords lie near the midline and cannot abduct, narrowing the airway, while their closeness still allows phonation.

steps.title: Lymphatics and laryngeal cancer
steps.text:
The vocal folds have hardly any lymphatics. Above them, the supraglottis is rich in lymphatics draining with the superior laryngeal vessels through the thyrohyoid membrane to the deep cervical nodes; below, the subglottis drains to pre- and paratracheal nodes.

A cancer of the vocal fold therefore changes the voice early and spreads to nodes late, while a supraglottic cancer is silent until it has often spread, sometimes to both sides of the neck.
steps.clinical: Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks, especially in a smoker, needs laryngoscopy.

check.q: Why does glottic cancer have a better prognosis than supraglottic cancer?
check.a: It causes hoarseness early, and the vocal folds have very few lymphatics, so it spreads to nodes late.
